newsitem.title: UK: MAM to warn off suitors with standby loan.
newsitem.headline: MAM to warn off suitors with standby loan.

text.p: Mercury Asset Management Plc's move to secure a standby loan to deal with any fund crisis sends a signal to potential bidders that it intends to fight to retain its independence, industry analysts said on Thursday.

Other independents could also follow suit, so reassuring clients that they could deal with a crisis like the one at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) last September when it was rocked by revelations of irregularities in three of its funds and the subsequent sacking of fund manager Peter Young, they said.
The 250 million stg standby loan demonstrated that it did not need the support a major ally if a problem arose.

"There is no point in doing this if they are about to throw in their lot with a mega-bank...There is no earthly point in trying to take over MAM unless you have the full support of the people who work there," Martin Cross, analyst at UBS.

BZW analyst Phillip Gibbs agreed MAM wanted to retain its independence. But he cautioned that: "clearly if someone wants to offer them an astronomic price they would have to consider it but the lesson is that although banks are interested in getting into fund management there is a certain constraint on the type of PE that they are prepared to pay."
At DMG, parent Deutsche Bank injected 180 million stg after the discovery of irregularities at the three funds.
It also announced a 200 million stg compensation package for investors who lost money.

MAM chairman Hugh Stevenson said in an interview the 250 million stg loan -- which MAM calls a precautionary line of credit and which is being arranged by mandated lead banks JP Morgan and Royal Bank of Scotland -- could have other purposes.
"You never know what you might need it for...It is a more efficient use of our resources to have the facility to borrow from banks.
"It is there in case you ever need it. That gives us the additional flexibility which we want to have.
Stevenson would not comment on the market speculation that the move was also designed to deter bidders.
He said there was no intention of drawing on the loan in the immediate future since MAM held a significant cash surplus.
Analysts also said other groups may look to a similar scheme, especially if it helped boost investor confidence.
"It is perfectly prudent and I am sure the bankers will be quite happy to do it," said Gibbs.
But he said the likelihood of MAM or any fund management group experiencing a crisis on the scale of DMG was extremely low.
Cross said groups which could consider a similar "insurance policy" included Schroders plc and M&G . Smaller operations were unlikely to see much benefit.
Regarding MAM, analysts said the share price, which was 39.5 pence down at 1,329 at 1520 GMT, may fall further as the speculative bid premium eased.
"It still has a takeover premium and is rather high on fundamental criteria," Cross said. But he said the premium may still hold as the market was determined to look for bid stocks.
Gibbs said the stock was likely to maintain a speculative premium, but it could come back "a bit further".
